messages.subject: Re: sample size
messages.body_plain:
It depends on a lot of factors: number of factors extracted, number of items, type of IRT model investigated (complexity matters; e.g., 3PL models are harder to estimate than 2PL), correlation of the latent traits, number of loadings within each trait, number of cross-loadings, and so on. Most of these relate to the number of parameters estimated, so more parameters generally require larger samples. Ultimately, like all pragmatic questions in statistics, the answer is "it depends", and offering some rule of thumb would be rather pointless and misleading. The best answer when considering sample size is to collect "as much quality data as you can practically obtain".

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Problems with my model using the graded reponse model
messages.body_plain:
This is an exploratory model, so I'm not sure what you mean when you are referring to the expected test score function (the function is subject to rotation, which may arbitrarily have negative loadings, and therefore can take on different orientations). You could try passing different rotations to the respective functions, but I generally think that if you have a good idea of what the structure should be you should change to a confirmatory model to avoid problems like this. In which case, you'll have to specify the factor loadings explicitly though a mirt.model() definition. Hope that helps.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: measurement invariance longitudinal IRT
messages.body_plain:
I think the strategy is to first establish confirmatory models before you try working on invariance across time points. Once that is done then you can more onto ways to compare across time points (check the wiki for some examples). This will probably be very difficult though given that your tests have 3 factors, as longitudinal IRT models tend to require additional dimensions to capture time-based effects.

Multiple group is for individuals in different groups who are completely independent, therefore this function should never be used for longitudinal analyses without great care. Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: measurement invariance longitudinal IRT
messages.body_plain:
Yes this seems justifiable, but it really depends on whether the structure should remain the same across time (for some scales this is fine, for others not so much). If theoretically the measures should have the same factor structure then this type of information is fine to collect. Just watch for things like flooring effects which may cause issues (think of a elementary math test used for individuals 10 and under, but given to university students.....everyone will get 100% most likely, so the structure may collapse due to the relatively extreme abilities). Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: intercet-slope to loading-threshold
messages.body_plain:
No definitely not, this requires changing from the c + aθ form to a(θ - b) form (which I have negative opinions about anyway), whereas the other transformation is into the standardized ogive metric, which is also slope-intercept. Check the code in mirt:::mirt2traditional for the correct transformation to the classical IRT form.

Phil

messages.subject: EFA for panel data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil

Please I have another question about running factor analysis for longitudinal data using MIRT. Is it possible to use one time point( say 2011) to run EFA and two time-points (2012 and 2013) to run CFA. I think about this approach beacause my sapmle size is small so I can't split it to cross-validate the model suggested by EFA and even if I split the data in each time point , the models suggested are not equivalent in the sense that items load differently in factors at each year leading to uncertainty about the best model to submit to confirmatory analysis.

Thanks again for your precious support!!
Makrem.

messages.subject: Debugging through the mirtCAT() function
messages.body_plain:
Hello Phil,

I was debugging mirtCAT() function using debug(mirtCAT) command to see how the next item selection works in case of multi dimensional items using Drule.

data(LSAT6)
data_LSAT6 = expand.table(LSAT6)

mod_LSAT6 = mirt(data = data_LSAT6, model = 2)

debug(mirtCAT)

CATdesign <- mirtCAT(df=NULL, mod_LSAT6,start_item = 'Drule', criteria = 'Drule',method = "ML" ,design_elements = TRUE, local_pattern = c(1,1,1,1,1))

While I was debugging it I came across Drule function which using ComputeCritera function internally. I need to go inside this function to see which parameters are taking which values.

Do you have any suggestions for me to how to debug an internal c++ function in R.

I know that I can not do it using RStudio. I have to use R from command line. I am doing that too; however it is not working it is throwing errors.

http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/src.html#src-debugging

I tries starting R from command prompt by using this command R --debugger=gdb

but it says:

unknown option '--debugger=gdb'

I have downloaded the gcc compiler and it works fine when I am compiling separate c++ files from command prompt.

I only need to ask how do you do it when you are building a R packages which has c++ functions inside,( if in case you are going wrong ) how do you debug them? Thank you very much, Irshad
